structure.title: The soldier and the city
structure.text: Food conflict and military danger introduce a community that needs Martius' courage while resisting his contempt.

structure.title: Recognition and refusal
structure.text: Political advancement tests whether military reputation can be translated into public consent. Personal pride meets institutions that can answer back.

context.title: Citizens and patricians
context.text: Class conflict concerns food, voice, and authority. Neither military service nor numbers automatically settles the dispute over rule.
context.takeaway: Follow the competing grounds of legitimacy.

context.title: Public performance
context.text: Seeking office requires showing and explaining merit to others. Martius treats parts of this process as degrading.
context.takeaway: Recognition must be received, not only deserved.

notice.text: Notice how wounds are displayed or withheld.

notice.why: Family admiration helps form public conduct.

opening: Rome's greatest soldier despises the citizens whose votes he needs. On the battlefield his courage is unquestionable; in public life he regards asking for approval as humiliation. His supporters want him to perform a little warmth, and his enemies know exactly how to provoke him. Shakespeare gives the city a defender who cannot bear the people he defends, and gives those people good reasons to distrust him. Military achievement becomes a dangerous qualification for governing when its owner treats disagreement as an insult to be crushed.
